author: Aidan Huang
title: People have to be treated as people
content:
From the airplane window, the land appeared almost uniformly yellow, stretched flat and uninterrupted beneath the wing. It was not the yellow of sunlight, but of dust and sand pressed into a vast plain, where roads were barely distinguishable from the earth around them. As the plane descended, the color did not change — it only grew closer. When the cabin door finally opened, heat rushed in immediately, dense and unapologetic, wrapping itself around the body before there was time to adjust. Outside, people moved through the glare wearing long sleeves, as if skin here had learned its own rules. Motorcycles dominated the roads, fast and loosely choreographed, riders weaving through traffic without helmets, without hesitation. Cars sped past on sand-colored streets, engines loud, windows open. I was driven through the city in a modest vehicle by a local professor — someone widely respected, I was later told — yet the ride itself felt precarious, carried forward by momentum more than by control. Only later did I begin to name the place where all of this was unfolding: N’Djamena, Chad.

Approaching N’Djamena from the air.

I had come here knowing that I would stay for two years. I was an early-career, female, Chinese researcher preparing for long-term fieldwork, and I arrived carrying not only academic plans but a quiet accumulation of unease. Before Chad, I had been based in North America, trying — often unsuccessfully — to prepare from afar. Emails to local academics were slow or unanswered. Online information was scarce and fragmented. What I knew instead came mostly through warnings: unstable electricity, unreliable internet, extreme heat, limited medical resources, and social norms that did not always favor women living alone. None of this was abstract to me. It translated quickly into practical anxieties — how to work, how to rest, how to remain functional without constantly negotiating risk. In that context, housing became the most urgent concern almost immediately. Before interviews, before archives, before learning how to move through the city with confidence, I needed a place where my body could settle, where nights were predictable, and where daily life did not consume all the energy meant for research.

In those first days, I made decisions less out of principle than out of necessity. I did not have the time — or the emotional capacity — to search extensively through unfamiliar networks, negotiate in a language I was still struggling to command, or assess safety across neighborhoods I could not yet read. The city was new, the social codes opaque, and my days already crowded with administrative tasks and introductions. When a Chinese contact offered help, it felt like a practical solution rather than a cultural statement. I assumed, perhaps too easily, that sharing a language and a background would reduce uncertainty. On my fourth day in Chad, I moved into a house rented by a Chinese businessman, Hang. The house was spacious, secure, and unusually well equipped by local standards. That night, I slept deeply for the first time since arriving. What the house offered was not luxury, but relief — a sense that daily life could run without constant vigilance. At that moment, convenience felt indistinguishable from safety, and safety was the foundation I needed to begin everything else.

Hang was a fellow Chinese around my age who had come here to build a life from scratch. In those first days, I read him as a compatriot trying to make it in a place where he was also exposed — linguistically, institutionally, and socially. I assumed that if he wanted to earn money here, he would also have to take my well-being seriously, because a long-term tenant only stays when life is stable. And in many ways, he did. Before a cook was even in place, he took me out almost every day for Chinese meals — expensive but consistently good — and that warmth mattered more than I expected. When I mentioned practical needs — hot water, a washing machine, taps that needed fixing, a trash bin — he tried to solve them, quickly and without hesitation. He stocked the house with drinks, fruit, and meat, and he had brought from China the rice noodles and grains I liked — things I could not easily find in local supermarkets. When he left for China, he even gave me emergency cash and handed me small items he thought I might need, like his hair dryer.

Surprisingly, however, what sustained me in those early weeks was a quiet coordination that formed …

author: Gboyega Ogundele
title: The Silk Drum
content:
Part One: The Arrival


In the year 1926, when the sun still climbed slow and steady over the red roofs of Ibadan, and the roads remained loyal to dust and earth, a man stepped off a creaking lorry with a chest of tea and a drum wrapped in silk. His name was Li Wei. His Mandarin name meant “strength and clarity,” but here in the sweltering market noise of a Yoruba town, names meant less than survival.


He stood still for a while, his pale robe gathering dirt around the hem, as he surveyed the open stalls, the scent of pepper and charcoal in the air, and the voices—singing, haggling, drumming—all clashing like waves. He had learned some English before the voyage but no Yoruba. Still, his father had said, “Listen first, then speak. The soul of trade is not in words but in silence and eyes.”


Li Wei rented a modest wooden stall at the edge of the market, shaded by an iroko tree. He unpacked the chests carefully. Inside were paper-tied bundles of oolong and pu-erh tea, dried hibiscus leaves, and a small red clay kettle. He placed the silk drum, still wrapped, beneath the table, away from sight.


Part Two: The Girl and the Drum


Adunni had always been drawn to rhythm. She did not speak it. She heard it. In the morning when the cock crowed, she listened to the way the sound bounced off the walls. When her mother pounded yam, Adunni matched the beat with her toes. Her father was a master drummer, his fingers like rivers flowing over goatskin, but he said a woman had no place with the talking drum.


One evening, as the last orange light slipped behind the palm trees, Adunni walked past the market stalls and heard something strange. Not the deep tone of Yoruba drums or the sharp clicks of agogo. This was softer, lighter, like rain on silk. She followed the sound and found the quiet trader sitting cross-legged in his stall, eyes closed, tapping on a round drum with threads along its sides. His fingers moved like breath.


She stayed hidden, watching.


The next evening, she returned. This time, she let a calabash fall so he would notice her. He did. He looked up and smiled, nodding politely. She pointed to the drum. He hesitated, then played a rhythm. She answered by tapping the side of the calabash. He laughed. She laughed.


They did not need words. Rhythm became their tongue.


Part Three: Tea and Talking Drums


Adunni began visiting every evening. Sometimes she brought him fried plantains wrapped in banana leaves. In return, he made tea. The first time she tasted it, she spat it out. It was bitter, earthy, confusing. But he showed her how to brew it properly—three breaths between the pour and the first sip. “Bitterness first,” he said slowly, pointing to his tongue. “Then sweet. Like life.”


She learned his name. He learned hers. She taught him to say “O da bo” when parting. He taught her to say “Zài jiàn.”


By the fourth week, she could mimic the Chinese rhythm he played. He began sketching her symbols—trees, moons, characters that looked like dancing legs. She showed him cowrie shells, songs, proverbs.


They crafted a new rhythm—hers from the village grove, his from distant mountains. They played in secret by the riverside. She closed her eyes and imagined her ancestors nodding in approval. He thought of his grandfather, who once told him, “Play to remember, not to impress.”


But not everyone approved.


Part Four: Drums of Disapproval


Rumours spread quickly in small towns. The elders whispered that Adunni had forgotten her place. Some said she had given her spirit to the foreigner. Her father summoned her.


“Why do you follow this man?”


“Because he listens.”


“A drummer listens to the spirits, not strangers.”


He forbade her from seeing Li Wei.


Meanwhile, a British officer visited Li Wei’s stall. He admired the tea, asked questions about his homeland, then warned him gently. “The Empire has eyes everywhere. Do not involve yourself in village matters. We value peace.”


Days later, Li Wei’s stall was raided by colonial soldiers. His tea was inspected, his papers scrutinised. The silk drum was taken.


Adunni cried when she heard.


That night, she crept into the colonial outpost, barefoot and trembling. Her cousin worked there as a cleaner. He helped her find the drum. She wrapped it in her shawl and ran like wind until she reached Li Wei’s hut.


She placed the drum before him.


He touched it as if touching memory. Then he looked at her and said one word: “Play.”


Part Five: The Farewell …

author: WoMin
title: Revisiting Ubuntu for our collective liberation
content:
Reflecting on the Afrocentric International Feminist Organising School


From 11 to 15 September 2026, the

Berta Caceres International Feminist Organising School (IFOS)

 convened in Nairobi, Kenya. Co-organised by the Grassroots Global Justice Alliance, the Indigenous Environmental Network, and the World March of Women, it brought together over 150 participants from 37 countries and territories. Grounded in a decolonial and Pan African vision, the programme created space to explore interconnected struggles and alternatives. Discussions centred on climate justice, agroecology, land rights, sovereignty, and the Nature Commons.


Ubuntu revisited


One of the running themes of the school was the philosophy of Ubuntu. Rooted in Southern African ways of life, Ubuntu is a living tradition that shapes how we relate to one another and to the world around us, both physical and spiritual. Ubuntu invites us to recognise one another’s personhood and our interdependence as part of the broader web of Life.


“Ubuntu is


often introduced through the phrase ‘umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’, commonly translated as ‘a person is a person through other people’ or simply


‘I am because we are’. Ubuntu calls us to see


personhood as fundamentally relational.


With Xenophobia and Afrophobia on the continent in service of right-wing agenda, we must reclaim Ubuntu.”-


Khwezilomso, South Africa


The school started from our individual journeys as feminists and the stories, struggles, and experiences that brought us to the movement. At the heart of these journeys was a deeper quest to reconnect with our own humanity, which in turn opened us to acknowledge and connect with the humanity of others. We came to see that, even before we could articulate it as such, the philosophy of Ubuntu was already present in our formation as feminists: the understanding that our humanity is deeply bound up with one another. From this recognition, we began to ask ourselves: What social projects, movements, ideas and philosophies can help us build ways of being that honour this interconnectedness?


Our questions have brought us into movements that challenge the imperialist ideologies and institutions that have disrupted and undermined Indigenous territories, cultures, and institutions. These include the anti-neoliberal movement, advanced by climate and ecological justice activists; the anti-imperialist movement, strengthened by decolonial thinkers and activists; and the anti-patriarchal movement, shaped by feminist struggles, etc. Across these movements, we find a shared commitment to transforming the systems that divide, exploit, and dehumanise us.


The tree of oppression


“White Supremacy needs excuses and pretexts to oppress people. [Systems of oppression] sustain their survival by eating our dignities.”

 –

Isabel, Senegal


As anti-migrant sentiment spreads across the continent, we are reminded that systems of oppression fuel separation, war, militarisation, and suspicion among communities. State policies rooted in carceral, and punitive logic turn people into enforcers of one another’s humanity, encouraging violence in the name of “justice”. This same violence polices and criminalises gender-expansive identities, mobilises mobs to attack women for how they dress, and displaces entire communities in the name of so-called development. We must therefore be careful not to confuse the effects of oppression with its roots.


Systems of oppression stand on ideologies that are not always visible, but that over time are normalised and turned into cultural norms, institutions, and policies and then, finally, are made visible through violent actions. Land theft; feminicide; privatisation of natural resources; predatory trade agreements; breaches of human rights; imposition of invasive biotechnologies and corporate-driven destruction are a partial catalogue of the violence caused by capitalism, colonialism and patriarchy.


(Tree of Resistance. Photo: World March of Women Kenya)


Not all is lost. The analysis drawn at the AFRO IFOS showed that, no matter how vast the dangers to our global communities, Indigenous peoples and their autonomy, it is no greater than the people’s power and commitment to sustain social, economic, political, cultural, and spiritual integrity. This was evidenced in the plethora of proposals and alternatives, as well as in the prayers, slogans, chants, music and dance that followed entire sessions.


Restoring our humanity


Through Ubuntu …

author: Fundi Skweyiya-Gushu
title: China’s Humanoid Robots: A New Test for African Technology Sovereignty
content:
For African governments, the significance of China’s humanoid-robotics programme is not that robots may one day appear on African battlefields. It is a diagnostic case of how a dual-use technology can move from commercial deployment to military relevance faster than the institutions responsible for assessing and governing it can adapt. Africa’s stake is therefore not speculative. African states already operate within global technology and defence supply chains dominated by external suppliers, including China. Humanoid robotics adds another layer to an existing problem, regarding how to acquire advanced technologies without becoming dependent on systems that governments cannot independently evaluate, secure or govern


That matters because humanoid robotics is not simply another consumer technology. It brings together artificial intelligence, machine perception, sensors, autonomous navigation, manipulation, communications and advanced manufacturing. Those capabilities can be developed for civilian purposes and subsequently adapted to military environments. The significance for Africa lies precisely in that movement across boundaries, because the continent enters this technological transition with substantial differences in technical, industrial and institutional capacity.


When civilian technology acquires military relevance


At last month’s World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, China’s Tiangong Ultra completed 100 metres in 8.64 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt’s human world record. Shortly afterwards, the People’s Liberation Army’s official newspaper discussed moving frontier robotics technologies from laboratories towards military training and described humanoid robots as potential “combatants”. The important point is not simply the robot’s performance. It is how quickly a technology demonstrated in a commercial and sporting setting can enter military thinking. That narrowing distance between civilian innovation and military application is precisely what African policymakers need to begin tracking.


China’s military interest in humanoid robots is no longer hypothetical. A Reuters investigation drawing on more than 100 Chinese military procurement notices, patents, academic papers and defence-industry records found research into applications including reconnaissance, logistics, hazardous environments and urban operations. Reuters found no evidence that armed humanoid robots have been deployed with an active PLA unit, while energy consumption and reliability remain significant technical constraints. The development is nevertheless important because China’s commercial robotics ecosystem is already providing an industrial base from which military applications can develop. Chinese manufacturers accounted for approximately 95% of global humanoid-robot shipments in 2025, according to BofA Global Research figures cited by Reuters. China is not alone in exploring military applications of humanoid systems, but its unusually large commercial manufacturing base gives the civil-military convergence particular significance.


Africa is not a bystander


For Africa, this convergence is occurring against an established pattern of technological and defence dependence. SIPRI’s latest data show that the United States, China, Russia and France collectively accounted for almost 60% of Africa’s major arms imports between 2021 and 2025, with China accounting for 17% of African major arms imports overall and 22% of those to sub-Saharan Africa. Africa is therefore not external to the global defence-industrial systems from which emerging capabilities are developing. It is already a significant recipient of technologies produced elsewhere.


This matters because the next generation of military-relevant technologies may not arrive through conventional defence procurement. A humanoid platform could enter an African market as a logistics, inspection, industrial or disaster-response system before acquiring military significance through changes to its software, sensors, communications architecture or operational role. The issue is consequently not whether African governments will suddenly purchase “robot soldiers”. It is whether procurement systems can recognise military relevance while a technology is still being classified and sold as civilian.


The dual-use problem


A conventional weapons platform is recognisable as a military asset when it is transferred, making its end use subject to established procurement, export-control and …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Defines Rights in Africa? Transnational Movements and the Unmaking of Human Rights
content:
Globally, hard-won rights and freedoms like sexual and reproductive health and rights, hate speech legislation that protects gender and sexual minorities, gender equality laws and the concept of gender itself, together with other progressive rights, are being challenged and rolled back. Africa, particularly, has become one of the battlegrounds for these contestations led by ultra-conservative groups and organisations identified as

anti-rights organisations

. These actors are considered ‘anti-rights’ not only because they contest established human rights norms, but also because they hold a different conception of rights rooted in European and religious ideas on tradition, protection and family. This is a regression of rights already hard-fought for in Africa, and it is often clothed in the language of sovereignty, African values and other seemingly neutral terms used to push harmful laws and policies that

target gender minorities

. These debates are fought at both domestic and international levels, and it is important to see how these actors construct narratives and use mechanisms that were created to enhance human rights protections to target those very rights. 


On 30 June 2026, Ordo Iuris (OI), a g

lobal Christian rights

 Polish-founded organisation, constituted its new

African arm

, Ordo Iuris Africa. 

It later 

announced

 that it

 had submitted a joint opinion to the UN Human Rights Council ahead of Uganda’s 4th cycle Universal Periodic Review (UPR), scheduled for October-November 2026. The Human Rights Council is an intergovernmental body which examines the human rights situation around the world through periodic meetings held in Geneva. The Council uses the UPR to continuously monitor the human rights situation in various countries and provide a platform for peer review amongst countries and feedback from various stakeholders, including civil society. The UPR is designed to be a mechanism through which states improve their human rights record and maintain international human rights standards.


Ordo Iuris’ choice of Uganda is not accidental, given previous and ongoing efforts to undermine the human rights of marginalised groups, best exemplified by the passing of the Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023. The law, described as one of

the harshest anti-LGBT laws globally

, carries sentences of up to life imprisonment and criminalises any advocacy or medical support relating to LGBTQ+ persons. Since its passage, human rights advocates have documented more than 1,000 cases of human rights violations against individuals and organisations identified or perceived as LGBTQ+ in nature in Uganda. Some activists have suggested a link between external transnational actors like OI and the legislation, as well as Uganda’s role in establishing the

African Inter-Parliamentary Conferences on Family Values and Sovereignty

 held in Entebbe for several years.


A month before the May 2026 submission, OI circulated a

112-question


survey

 to government ministries, civil society organisations, and religious bodies across Africa, ostensibly to inform its report to the United Nations. It is absurd that an organisation that has previously worked primarily in Poland in the European context is attempting to use its Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) consultative status at the UN to make policy recommendations for Uganda or any other African country. Although Ordo Iuris describes its submission as a defence of family, parental rights, child protection, religious freedom, and national sovereignty, its track record in this terrain gives us cause for pause.


In recent years, there has been a rollback of hard-won human rights protections in these areas in various African countries, including the rejection of age-appropriate comprehensive sexual education, further criminalisation of minoritised communities, and the weaponisation of “sovereignty” language to weaken civil society. A careful reading of OI’s past

documented positions

 across these five areas suggests a pattern of selective treaty citation and normative inversion that poses an even further risk to the implementation of international human rights law in Uganda and across the African continent.


Flags outside the United Nations Office in Geneva under a clear blue sky. Pexels Photo.


Capturing the United Nations systems from the Inside


The Human Rights Council-led UPR is one of the most important accountability mechanisms in international human rights law. The …

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 


Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt.

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       


In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.


An anthropological base map of Plateau Province reproduced from C.G. Ames, The Gazetteers of Plateau Province, 1932 (Copy in Nigerian National Archives, Kaduna)


The highlands were ideal for the crop. Potatos thrive in cooler conditions, and Jos and Mambila provided the climate colonial agronomists desired. However, these areas were not empty spaces waiting for improvement. They were inhabited, farmed, and politically complex societies with their own crops, markets, and knowledge systems.


Colonial rule altered the dynamics in these regions. Tin mining on the Jos Plateau attracted workers, administrators, and settlers. Demand for European foods increased. Potatos, once a garden crop for expatriates and mission stations, began to seem valuable to the colonial state.


Starting in the 1930s, British

officials based in Nigeria began importing seed potatos from Ireland, Britain, Europe, South Africa, the Canary Islands, and the United States.

 Mission stations cultivated the potatos. District heads distributed the seed. Farmers cautiously tried the crop, incorporating it into local routines where it made sense while rejecting it when it didn’t. The potato became a means of power.


This did not mean that older crops and seed systems disappeared. There was no formal ban, and local farmers continued to grow, save, and exchange seed in various ways. The scheme worked in subtler ways: it altered the rewards. Access to land, labour, credit, official support, and markets began to favour the colonial crop. Imported seed was seen as improved, while farmer-saved seed and local knowledge were pushed to the sidelines. Over time, diverse and adaptable seed systems were narrowed, though not completely erased, by a supply chain prioritising mines, mission stations, military demands, and imperial markets.


Before the Second World War, the scheme was no great success. Some farmers thought potatos were poisonous. Others saw no reason to cultivate a crop with a limited, European-dominated market. A 1937 attempt to sell imported ‘Great Scott’ seed potatos to the Jos Native Authority ended poorly: half went unsold, the remainder was given away, and the scheme lost money.


War transformed failure into urgency. The empire needed food close to military outposts. It aimed to save cargo space and lessen reliance on disrupted shipping routes. Suddenly, potatos on the Mambila and Jos Plateau became crucial.


The war economy and the creation of dependency


Production surged from around

90 tons at the beginning of the war in 1939 to about 1,200 tons by 1943. Seed stores and experimental stations emerged throughout Kagoro, Zonkwa, Kurmin Biri, and Riyom

. Colonial science advanced rapidly, too: London-based Kew scientists devised ways to transport sprouting ‘eyes’ of potatos instead of whole tubers, facilitating a steady supply from outside.


Wartime officials did not establish an independent Nigerian seed system; they created a supply chain. Farmers were encouraged to boost production. Yet, this authority remained elsewhere: seed, disease control, imports, and markets remained …

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu congress adjourned after credential dispute exposes tensions
content:
The Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) has adjourned its 15

th

 national congress after seven affiliates withheld their delegate credentials, preventing the federation from reaching the quorum required to proceed with the meeting.


The decision, announced after two days of difficult proceedings, brought the congress to a halt before delegates could debate the federation’s political report, organisational matters and resolutions affecting workers.


Speaking to

Elitsha

 outside the congress venue on Wednesday, Cosatu spokesperson Zanele Sabela said the decision by some affiliates not to submit their credentials was linked primarily to the suspension of Cosatu’s first deputy president, Mike Shingange, by his union, the National Education, Health and Allied Workers’ Union (Nehawu), shortly before the congress.


Sabela said the suspension had become a “bone of contention” because affiliates wanted clarity on why Shingange had been suspended on the eve of the congress and whether the move would prevent his candidacy for a leadership position. Nehawu’s general secretary clarified in the congress that the suspension was an internal union matter and did not mean Shingange could not stand for a Cosatu position. She said Shingange remained a shop steward and a member of an affiliated union.


The dispute was also taken to the Labour Court. Sabela said the court ruled on Tuesday night that the suspension did not stand, making the issue of his immediate suspension a moot point in relation to the congress.


Shingange himself told journalists that the reasons for his suspension were a matter between himself and his union. He also maintained that a person seeking a leadership position in Cosatu must meet the federation’s membership requirements.


Four Cosatu affiliates – Sadtu, Nehawu, Popcru and Sactwu – had organised a separate press conference outside of its mother body but it was later cancelled. Photo by Simon Ramapuputla


Cosatu denies clear divisions


The suspension and credential dispute unfolded alongside dissent among affiliates, with four unions calling a press briefing outside the Cosatu congress but cancelled it. Cosatu’s leadership played down the significance of the separate briefing, saying it should not be interpreted as evidence that the federation was fragmenting. They insisted disagreements among affiliates were not new and that similar tensions had been managed in previous congresses. Discussions among leaders during the two-day gathering, they argued, showed that the affiliates were not necessarily as far apart as the events at the congress suggested.


The precise reasons and positions that the four affiliates intended to advance at their separate media briefing were not fully addressed by Cosatu’s national office bearers during the federation’s own briefing. The issue was, however, part of the wider dispute about credentials, the suspension of Shingange and the conduct of the congress.


Cosatu’s leadership said seven unions attending the congress had not submitted their credential lists. Without those lists, the federation could not establish the number of eligible delegates for purposes of calculating a quorum. National office bearers said the congress spent roughly three hours dealing with the issue before the constitutional limit was reached. Under clause 3.4 of the federation’s constitution, the congress had to be adjourned and the president is required to reconvene it within 30 days.


So, the ultimate reason for the adjournment, was this technicality rather than a substantive political disagreement over the direction of the federation.


“We do not want to confirm what we cannot prove,” one of the leaders told journalists when asked whether political interests had influenced the events at the congress. The political questions that were supposed to dominate the congress included Cosatu’s relationship with the ANC and the SACP, particularly after the SACP’s decision to contest the upcoming local government elections independently.


The issue has implications for the tripartite alliance, which brings together the ANC, Cosatu and the SACP. Although the three organisations retain their decision-making processes, the ANC has long dominated its partners. During the briefing, Cosatu leaders stressed that the SACP was an independent organisation entitled to take its own decisions.


At the same time, Cosatu had been expected to debate the implications of the SACP’s electoral strategy …

author: Deogracious Kalima
title: Young Zimbabweans are being “kidnapped” and sent to rehab camps. Former detainees say they were tortured inside
content:
Former detainees say they were tortured inside.

Harare, Zimbabwe (Minority Africa) â

In the heart of Mbare Township, Harareâs poorest and most populated slum, there is a new and menacing economy emerging.

âItâs the drug trade and itâs on steroids,â says John Gwada, a community leader and pastor with the Zimbabwe Apostolic Church. Zimbabweâs youth substance abuse crisis has skyrocketed from 43% in 2017 to 57% in 2019, and is believed to be much worse today, according to the Zimbabwe Civil Liberties and Drugs Network, a monitoring agency.

This new dark-street economy is built on the broken lives of Zimbabweâs so-called âLost Generationââyoung adults born after 2000 who are the demographic most affected by the countryâs dire unemployment crisis. In 2023, researchers, citing social workers and addiction specialists, reported that 43% of school-going youths were hooked on illicit substances ranging from crystal meth (locally known as mutoriro) to tainted cough syrups and imported cocaine.

âItâs a mess, kids abandoning school, some chasing their parents out of their homes, others selling all the household furniture just to buy the next supply and feed their cravings for mutoriro,â Gwada says.

But the real horror isn't just found in the âstreet bases,â where the drugs are sold in small sachets and makeshift beer bottles. It lies behind the immaculate, steel-wire fences of so-called ârehab boot campsâ that claim to reform youths battling addictions, all for free.

Our investigation into Zimbabweâs mushrooming âdrug rehabilitationâ hubs shows that they have become a cesspool of corruption and brutality, where politically connected elites have turned a public health crisis into a money-spinning racket.

At centres such as Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, which began working around 2021/2022, and the Angel of Hope Foundation, established in Harare in 2018, former detainees and their families allege that the road to sobriety involves cash bribes, military-style torture, unlawful detention, and the disregard of basic human rights.

To a desperate parent such as Chipo Ganga*, watching her 17-year-old son waste away through mutoriro addiction, it didnât take much to fall for the sleek adverts on TikTok and Facebook promoting Zimbabweâs âdrug rehab colleges.â

âI was desperate to save my teenage son in 2025, the rehab adverts looked godsend,â she says.

The advertisements promise âholistic therapy,â âpsychological assessments,â and a path back to sanity, education, or employment for âsaved youths.â In Zimbabwe, where the formal healthcare system has all but collapsed and only 18 psychiatrists reportedly serve a population of 17 million, these seemingly non-profit rehabilitation centres pose as the only remaining hope for parents whose children are addicted to crystal meth, cocaine, illicit alcohol, or other narcotics.

The Matrix Rehabilitation Centre, owned by Tafadzwa Chidawa, a politically connected former police officer who was acquitted in March last year of an unrelated US $20,000 fraud case, and Angel of Hope, a foundation headed by Zimbabweâs First Lady, Auxillia Mnangagwa, are the most prominent of these so-called ârehab colleges.â

They claim to offer free or subsidised programmes lasting between one and three months to transform young people battling addiction into productive members of society.

But Matrixâs pitch extends beyond rehabilitation. In videos and advertisements reviewed by Minority Africa, the centre presents its programmes as a pathway to opportunities after participants leave, including education and travel abroad. Posts promote opportunities in countries including India and the United Arab Emirates, while others document participants obtaining visas and travelling overseas to study.

In one video posted in August 2026, Matrix celebrated a young woman receiving a visa to study abroad, before later chronicling her journey to India. The posts present such departures as evidence of what can follow the centreâs disciplinary programme.

Matrix has made varying claims about the success of its rehabilitation programme. In separate posts on social media, the centre has claimed success rates of 92% and 97%. The posts do not explain how Matrix defines âsuccess,â the period over which participants are followed, or what data the figures are based on.

author: Mariam Soliman
title: Court upholds sentence against Omnia Sweidan for publishing description of obstetric violence at Al-Shatby Hospital
content:
Omnia Sweidan’s appeal against a fine and prison sentence she received for a Facebook post describing abuses against patients was rejected on Thursday, according to her lawyer Ahmed Ragheb. 


Sweidan was tried earlier this year on charges relating to the post which detailed obstetric and other forms of violence against women at Alexandria’s Al-Shatby Hospital. A misdemeanor court ultimately

issued

 her with a six-month prison sentence and a LE20,000 fine. The prison sentence was issued with a three-year suspension. 


Ragheb told Mada Masr that after he attended her hearing at the Economic Misdemeanors Court at Dekheila Courthouse this week, the court rejected her appeal and upheld the

July

 ruling.


Sweidan’s post described instances of physical and sexual abuse of women patients at Alexandria University’s Al-Shatby Hospital. Sweidan recounted incidents she said she had witnessed or heard discussed during her medical training in the hospital’s obstetrics and gynecology department six years earlier.


The post went viral within hours and drew tens of thousands of

shares

 and comments amid a conversation that quickly turned to other instances of obstetric violence, with many

women

 sharing their own experiences of mistreatment in maternity wards.


Healthcare professionals who spoke to Mada Masr

said

 the abuses she recounted reflected a common and pervasive reality in public hospitals.

 


The head of legal affairs at Alexandria University Hospitals subsequently filed a

complaint

 against Sweidan, citing concerns over the hospitals’ reputation.

 


Sweidan was

arrested

 from her home in Damanhour on June 16, one day after publishing the testimony, and was later released on LE20,000 bail following questioning by prosecutors.

 


The prosecution subsequently referred her to the Economic Misdemeanors Court on charges of deliberately broadcasting false news, using an electronic account to commit a crime and publishing false news.


The misdemeanor court ultimately convicted Sweidan in June on the charges of publishing false news and intentionally spreading false news, while acquitting her at the same time on a separate charge of using a social media account to commit a crime. 


The court also excluded a provision of the cybercrime law concerning violations of Egyptian family values from the case.

The post

Court upholds sentence against Omnia Sweidan for publishing description of obstetric violence at Al-Shatby Hospital

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Ayoola Babalola
title: Too big to regulate
content:
In September 2024, Nigeria achieved something it had been promised for decades: the Dangote Petroleum Refinery began producing petrol on Nigerian soil. At 650,000 barrels per day,

the largest single-train refinery on earth

, it was a genuine industrial landmark.

Yet, by early 2026, Nigerian consumers were paying petrol prices roughly 12 percent above what competitive imports would have cost, according to a shelved

World Bank report

.

It is well argued by

scholars

 that Nigerian merchant capital did not emerge organically from agricultural surpluses or small manufacturing. It was shaped, from the colonial era onward, by three distinctive features: import-substitution policies that protected specific domestic interests; an oil economy that concentrated state revenues in few hands; and a “political settlement,” in the words of economist and professor Mushtaq Khan, that tied business access to political proximity rather than competitive performance.

The

Dantata

 family were among the trading families of northern Nigeria, enriched under colonial commodity boards that set paltry prices paid to farmers for export crops, with the boards accumulating surpluses that sometimes exceeded 100 percent of expected earnings. Licensed Buying Agents extracted their own share between the farmgate and export terminal. Farmers received the smallest portion of the value their labor produced. Aliko Dangote, Dantata’s great-grandson, is the chairman of Dangote Industries Ltd.

Nigeria’s “backward integration policy,” launched in 2002 to develop domestic manufacturing through tariff protection and tax incentives, was sound in principle. In practice, the political settlement governing it systematically concentrated its benefits in conglomerates with pre-existing political access. Nigeria’s industrial policy became a form of legislated primitive accumulation where the state manufactured the conditions for monopoly capital to form, and connected families captured those conditions first.

Nigeria’s cement capacity grew from roughly 2 million to nearly 48 million metric tonnes per annum between 2002 and 2019. Dangote invested in massive-scale kilns that outcompeted rivals, developed coal-mining operations to cut fuel costs, negotiated machinery discounts from Chinese contractors, and maintained a cost-to-revenue ratio of 30 to 40 percent against Lafarge Nigeria’s 70 to 80 percent. By Schumpeterian standards, this was a genuine competitive success.

But between 2011 and 2016, Dangote Cement’s profits more than tripled, whereas average wages per employee, over the same period,

fell in real terms

. The effective corporate tax rate on Nigerian cement operations was approximately 2 percent in 2016, against a statutory 30 percent. This was achieved by continuously rolling “pioneer status” tax holidays across new production lines as previous exemption windows expired.

Between 2010 and 2017, Dangote Cement earned NGN 1.7 trillion in profits and paid NGN 90 billion in taxes: a realized rate of roughly 5 percent

.

The “paradox of costs” holds that while rising wages reduce individual firm margins, they increase aggregate demand and, ultimately, total profit rates across the economy. A monopolist that suppresses wages and minimizes its fiscal contribution may maximize its own returns while shrinking both the purchasing power its sales depend on and the state resources needed to sustain it. When commodity prices fell in 2014, and Nigerian consumer spending contracted sharply, DIL’s food-processing businesses showed signs of this structural overcapacity: markets created by policy, but without the wage growth to sustain them.

Still, Dangote Refinery represents a qualitative leap in strategic importance. Its capacity reportedly

exceeds Nigeria’s entire domestic fuel demand

. Practically, it now supplies about 62 percent of Nigeria’s petrol, becoming the main supplier after import licenses were restricted. The monopoly emerged as failed state refineries and excluded modular operators left a technically superior but politically difficult private monopoly replacing a corrupt state one.

The “crude-for-naira” arrangement inaugurated in October 2024 is the analytical crux of the “fair deal” question. Despite its name, the scheme is not a simple currency substitution. It is not merely barter.

NNPC supplies crude to Dangote in naira; Dangote, in return, sells the refined equivalent of the received product to Nigerian market(ers) in naira

. Though …

author: David Venn
title: Ottawa police seek public’s help in locating 12-year-old girl
content:
Ottawa police are asking the public for help in locating a 12-year-old girl.


Emily Koonoo was last seen at 5:30 p.m. on Wednesday, in Ottawa’s Greenboro East neighbourhood, according to an Ottawa Police Service news release.


“There are concerns for her health and safety,” the release says.


She was last seen wearing grey pants, a black sweater and black shoes. Police described her as Indigenous, 4’10, and weighing about 90 lbs. She has black hair, brown eyes and nose and ear piercings, according to the release.


The police asked anyone with information on her whereabouts to call 613 236 1222, extension 7300.


When asked by Nunatsiaq News, the Ottawa Police Service could not confirm if Koonoo is Inuk.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: Federal agency postpones release of report on B.C. RCMP until after election
content:
A federal watchdog is postponing the release of its report on the RCMP’s specialized protest response unit in British Columbia.


The new report by the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission (CRCC) into the

Critical Response Unit BC (CRU-BC),

 was to be released Wednesday, but the agency said it won’t be released until after the B.C. provincial election, called Tuesday by Premier David Eby.


“During an election period, the provincial government operates under caretaker conventions, which limit its ability to address or respond to matters that could be viewed as involving policy, administration, or future government decision-making. Publishing the report while the province is in caretaker mode would therefore make it difficult for the relevant provincial authorities to fully consider and respond to its findings and recommendations,” said an email from the CRCC.


“To ensure the report receives appropriate consideration and to avoid any perception of interference in the election period, we have decided to delay publication until a new government has been sworn in and normal government operations have resumed.”


CRU-BC is the new name for the Community-Industry Response Group, or C-IRG, which the RCMP adopted in 2024.


The CRCC is a federal agency, separate from the RCMP, that investigates complaints from the public about the conduct of the Mounties. According to its website, the agency “conducts reviews when complainants are not satisfied with the RCMP’s handling of their complaints.”


The agency shared an embargoed copy of the report with APTN News after the network agreed “not to publish any information from this report until its official release.” At least one other network agreed to the same terms, which is common with upcoming reports. Advance copies allow news outlets to analyse a report prior to its release.


The CRCC initiated the systemic investigation after receiving more than 500 public complaints, as well as letters from civil liberties groups, Indigenous organizations, interested parties and people directly impacted, according to a statement from the agency in March.


The C-IRG was established by the B.C. RCMP in 2017 to address the increasing number of protests related to resource-based development projects, such as pipelines and logging operations.


Its primary purpose was “intended to provide strategic oversight in addressing energy industry (gas and oil pipeline) incidents and related public order, national security and crime issues. Its mandate was to ensure a consistent, standardized and impartially administered police response across the province, using a measured approach in facilitating the peaceful resolution of public order issues,” according to the RCMP website.


The C-IRG’s operations on Wet’suwet’en territory in 2020 prompted backlash and countrywide protests like this one in Ottawa. Photo: APTN


‘Bewildering’ 


The president of the Canadian Association of Journalists (CAJ), an organization that represents journalists in Canada, called the decision to withhold the report until after the election “bewildering.”


“C-IRG has been the subject of intense scrutiny from the public and press freedom advocates for many years due to its repeated use of so-called ‘exclusion zones’ during demonstrations over the development of natural resource projects in Wet’suwet’en territory and Fairy Creek. These tactics have been deemed to have caused “serious interference” with press freedoms,” Brent  Jolly said.


Jolly said an election shouldn’t be a reason not to release the report.


“As an independent watchdog, however, it appears the CRCC is making what amounts to a political decision by withholding this report. The public’s right to know is a fundamental principle of a free and democratic society. Transparency matters because accountability depends on the public having access to information about decisions, institutions, and matters of legitimate public concern.


“Withholding this report today hurts the public’s ability to receive a dispassionate analysis about the conduct of agencies funded by taxpayer dollars and, ultimately, to hold power to account,” he said.


According to an update on the status of C-IRG-related public complaints and reviews (as of March 1, 2026) on the CRCC website, of the 572 public complaints received by the CRCC, only 123 met the complaint criteria laid out in section 45.53 of the

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act

.


The CRCC said that most of the refused …

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: Don’t Be Fooled: GOP Scuffle Over NIH Grants Doesn’t Mean Science Has Prevailed
content:
Trump has backed down for now in his new bid to control research grants, but his tune could change after the midterms.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Over the last two years, in an effort to stamp its ideology on the country’s premier academic and scientific institutions, the Trump administration has repeatedly moved to exert control over how grants from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) are distributed.

According to reporting by The New York Times and other outlets, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), led by Russell Vought, was recently involved in drafting an executive order for Donald Trump to sign that would create an overview board with the power to veto NIH grants that do not conform with the administration’s political priorities.

When the story about the proposed executive order broke, several senators — including Susan Collins, who is facing a tough reelection fight — immediately announced their opposition to this power grab and made it clear they would do everything in their power to block it. Days later, faced with this opposition, the administration announced it was withdrawing the proposal. What it refused to do, however, was promise not to reintroduce some form of it down the road, quite possibly after the midterm elections. As a result, the Damocletian sword of political influence continues to hang over the world of medical research.

Given the administration’s dismal track record when it comes to scientific freedom, and its ongoing hostility to much of the NIH apparatus, it seems unlikely to have permanently and tamely given up the fight to expand control over the grantmaking process.

The annual NIH budget currently stands at just over $47 billion. Since Trump took office again in January 2025, there have been significant slowdowns in the approval and distribution of grants, and the administration has sought to slash NIH spending — a move that, to date, Congress has rejected. In its latest budget request, the administration asked for $41 billion to fund the NIH next year, representing more than a 10 percent cut to its budget.

Team Trump frequently talks about the need to “streamline” public health and research budgets. In reality, it is using expansive budget cuts at the NIH and elsewhere as a cudgel to eradicate any grants that study disparate impacts of disease and of medical interventions on different economic, racial, and sexual groups, and it is slowing down the awarding of competitive grants as a way to coerce research institutions to toe the new party line. Earlier this year, in the wake of the DOGE-related purges to the NIH and other grant-making agencies, the University of California, Davis’s Office of Research reported that nationally, the awarding of competitive NIH grants had dropped off by more than 50 percent since Trump’s inauguration.

On September 16, facing a second wave of cuts, a group of researchers sued the NIH, claiming that the agency is using a group of 235 keywords — each of which relates to diversity, equity, and climate change issues — to ferret out suspect projects, and is systematically rejecting grant applications containing those words. The suit, which also involves the ACLU and the Protect Democracy Project, was filed in federal court in San Francisco and alleges that “researchers with existing NIH grants or pending applications are now subjected to an algorithmic screen for a list of 235 disfavored terms that serve as proxies for the disfavored viewpoints, including ‘gender,’ ‘equity,’ ‘diverse,’ ‘racist,’ ‘queer, ‘trans,’ and ‘climate change.’ NIH requires the removal of all flagged terms upon threat of termination or funding denial. Researchers must instead parrot NIH’s preferred phrasing in public-facing grant materials, limiting researchers’ ability to communicate clearly about their work to the public and to each other in a manner consistent with their viewpoint.”

This beatdown of researchers and research institutions has led to the termination of hundreds of projects, including grants for projects the descriptions of which contained the phrases “health equity,” “climate change,” or “workforce diversity.” The Trump administration’s new rules have also terminated projects investigating sexual harassment, which is allegedly categorized as “DEI-related,” and led to the end of longstanding grants to researchers studying Alzheimer’s disease in lower-income Black …

author: Unknown
title: "Never Again": Czechoslovakian Hardcore in the Syrian Civil War
content:
In the following narrative, anarchists who participated as internationalist volunteers in the fight to defend Rojava against the Islamic State describe the role that the anti-militarist song “Už Nikdy” (“Never Again”) by the Czechoslovakian hardcore band Kritická Situace played in their experience.


This text is adapted from the newest issue of the anarchist hardcore publication

Inside Front

.

 We share it here to explore the importance of revolutionary music and culture in social movements.

The personal is geopolitical.


These events took place in March 2019, near the end of the fight against the Islamic State. At that time, the Turkish army and its Syrian proxies had brutally seized the majority-Kurdish district of Afrin in northwest Syria, and Donald Trump was

signaling

 that he would permit them to attack the rest of Rojava as well. At the same time, the Islamic State still controlled territory in Deir Ezzor in the southeast, where the final battles took place at al-Baghuz Fawqani.


As soon as the Islamic State was defeated, the United States government gave Turkey the green light to

butcher

 those who had defeated it. In 2024,

Turkish-backed forces

 came to power in Syria, creating

new challenges

 for the multiethnic revolutionary experiment in Rojava. Nonetheless, the fight for free life continues—in Rojava and the

rest

 of Syria, in

Turkey

, in Czech Republic and Slovakia, and even in the United States.

The struggle continues.


“Už Nikdy” by Kritická Situace.


We received the following accounts of the same events from two different correspondents.


Account I. — “Never Again”


In March 2019, I was in Syria, an internationalist volunteer in the midst of the civil war.


We were fighting on two fronts. To the northwest, our comrades were locked in a defensive war with Turkish proxies and the Turkish state itself, whereas we were engaged in an offensive war with Daesh in the southeast. To the northwest, death from above: snipers and drones. In the southeast, death from below: snipers and mines.


My friends and I were positioned on the second floor of an abandoned building in the ruins of the town of Al-Baghuz Fawqani. A Tweety Bird blanket was hung over one of the blacked-out windows in our room. There was a small kitten who would sleep with us. The comrades in the hospital to the north had sent us there with an ambulance. We took it forward to retrieve casualties from the front line, administering what care we could. Usually, I drove.


This cat briefly held the most advantageous position in the Syrian civil war.


In our group, there were volunteers from around the world who had come to Syria to defend the revolution. We found ourselves there in the last days of the last battle of the territorial war against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. In our ambulance unit, none of us shared common citizenship or a native tongue, but we soon found that we did share a background in the global punk counterculture.


One of the comrades described to me the sadness he had felt on the day that he had been forced to shave off his mohawk and flee his country. “But punk is not here,” he said, pointing at his hair. “It is here,” he said, pressing his fist to his heart.


“A Tweety Bird blanket was hung over one of the blacked-out windows in our room.”


By leaving my phone on the roof for several hours, I had managed to download a song titled “Never Again,” recorded in 1992 by the Czechoslovakian band

Kritická Situace

. The song had come to my attention in the year 1998, when it was featured in a memorable and impassioned review in

issue 11

 of the North American hardcore publication

Inside Front.

 It tells the story of a conscript fleeing from the army
through the wilderness, vowing that his superiors will never be able to force him to kill.


My friends and I were now in the exact inverse of that situation: we were internationalists who had crossed the world voluntarily to defend the principles of autonomy, ecology, and women’s liberation that the social movements in northeastern Syria were putting into practice. Still, war
is war. Many nights, after

tekmil

, we would sing “Never Again” together quietly in the darkness, to the sound of gunfire, mortar fire, and bombs. Those fluent in Slavic languages would sing the words, and the rest of us would carry the rhythms and harmonies as best we could.


In a dark dungeon, in the glow of torches,


You hide from the exercise of power.


You do not …

author: Bianca Blell
title: Virginia Voters Will Decide the Future of Reproductive Freedom, Marriage Equality, and Voting Rights This November
content:
On November 3rd, Virginia voters will decide on three proposed amendments to the state constitution concerning reproductive freedom, marriage, and voting rights. The amendments would add a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, remove Virginia’s constitutional prohibition on same-sex marriage and require equal treatment of marriages, and automatically restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release of incarceration.

Together, the measures represent one of the most consequential ballot slates for civil rights in the state’s recent history, including a rare opportunity for voters to enshrine protections directly into the state constitution, beyond the reach of a hostile legislature or a change in administration. All three amendments were approved by the General Assembly through Virginia’s constitutional amendment process and will appear on the November 2026 ballot.

The first amendment establishes a constitutional right to reproductive freedom and access. The amendment defines the right as including decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility care. It would also prohibit the Commonwealth from penalizing or prosecuting individuals for exercising those rights, as well as doctors, nurses, and others who assist patients with their voluntary consent.

The question voters will see on the ballot:

“Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; (ii) protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and (iii) allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient’s health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?”

If passed, this would make Virginia’s protections some of the most durable in the South, solidifying it as the last Southern state without an abortion ban. This status would keep reproductive rights safe from the current legislature but also from whoever holds the governor’s office next. In a state where 8,570 people traveled from states like Georgia, Florida, and North Carolina in 2025 to receive healthcare, establishing reproductive access has never been more important. Virginia voters can impact generations to come in a Post-Dobbs environment.

The second amendment would remove the Virginia Constitution’s existing language stating that only a union between one man and one woman may be recognized as a valid marriage. It would replace that language with a provision stating that marriage is one of the vital personal rights essential to the orderly pursuit of happiness.

The official ballot question asks:

“Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) remove the ban on same-sex marriage; (ii) affirm that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race; and (iii) require all legally valid marriages to be treated equally under the law?”

Same-sex marriage has been legally recognized in Virginia since 2014 following a federal court ruling, and the U.S. Supreme Court recognized a constitutional right to same-sex marriage nationwide in Obergefell v. Hodges that same year. Virginia’s Constitution, however, still contains language prohibiting same-sex marriage. The proposed amendment would remove that language and establish equal treatment of legally valid marriages in the state constitution.

If approved, the amendment would take effect January 1, 2027.

The third amendment would automatically restore voting rights to formerly incarcerated Virginians once they are released from prison and complete any additional required steps, such as parole or probation. Currently, Virginia is one of the few states where a person with a felony conviction must individually petition the governor to have their voting rights restored, producing a discretionary, case-by-case process which rights restoration advocates have long called arbitrary and disenfranchising.

The ballot question asks voters:

“Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the …

author: Kevin Carson
title: Ruthanna Emyrs, A Half-Built Garden, Tor 2022
content:
Recensione a cura di

Kevin Carson

. Originale:

A Half-Built Garden, by Ruthanna Emrys (Tor 2022)

, del 29 luglio 2026. Traduzione italiana di

Enrico Sanna

.


A Half-Built Garden

 è una storia di contatto alieno ben congegnata, dalla trama avvincente, cose che da sole fanno una piacevole lettura. Come forse saprà chi ha già letto altre mie recensioni, quando recensisco storie di fantascienza ambientate in un futuro prossimo utopico, libero e postcapitalista, il mio interesse riguarda anche come questo mondo è strutturato. Un peccatuccio che condivido con Auden che scrive ispirandosi alla bibbia.


Siamo negli anni 2080, dopo l’Età delle Turbolenze di metà secolo, e il mondo emerge dalle rovine del capitalismo per creare una nuova, tollerabile società.


La principale istituzione di governo è la watershed network, una federazione di istituzioni locali autogestite grossomodo corrispondenti alle bioregioni, comprendente gran parte della popolazione e delle risorse mondiali. L’equilibrio di potere è il risultato di una rivoluzione perlopiù nonviolenta iniziata una o due generazioni prima e finita verso il 2050: una serie di boicottaggi, sabotaggi e altre azioni dirette spingono le aziende economiche a rinchiudersi in enclave in alto mare. La vicenda è narrata attraverso gli occhi di un abitante della Chesapeake Watershed, che ricorda quando i suoi genitori “mettevano i primi sensori vietati nel fiume Potomac e barricavano le fabbriche per imporre la volontà collettiva della nascente rivoluzione dandelion.”


Le aziende sono perlopiù “padroni miliardari e dipendenti servi ammassati dietro il filo spinato nelle loro isole artificiali.” Tranne “qualche convertito e visitatore”, gli abitanti sono “i discendenti delle persone arrivate con il loro fondatore: dipendenti e sodali che preferivano scappare dall’apocalisse piuttosto che unirsi in comunità e evitarla.”


Le enclave aziendali sono circondate da “filo spinato” evidentemente imposto dalle watershed durante la rivoluzione. “Finalmente abbiamo vietato le aziende. Mio padre e altri, che hanno dato vita alla prima rete del cambiamento, hanno operato per fermarle.” La rivoluzione “limita la produzione di CO

2

 per contenere il riscaldamento climatico bloccando i trasporti quando si supera il limite.” Le aziende, “refrattarie al cambiamento, … finiscono per barricarsi dietro il filo spinato in alcune isole artificiali…”


Esiliate nelle isole, gran parte delle aziende, che “già da tempo hanno perso ogni parvenza di legalità”, rifiuta qualunque riconoscimento ufficiale dalle watershed. Inviano osservatori ai dialoghi sulla CO

2

, obbediscono tacitamente alle limitazioni dell’anidride e di altri inquinanti che le watershed, attori principali, impongono loro, e imbrogliano pensando di poter sfuggire ai controlli. Data la loro relativa debolezza, sono costrette a chiedere il permesso delle watershed consorziate quando l’impatto delle loro attività supera i confini.


Gran parte delle funzioni economiche delle società, tolte alcune zone che hanno ancora il monopolio del know-how, sono state rilevate dalle watershed. Comprese certe istituzioni industriali risalenti al periodo precedente, come il “MIT e l’Associazione di costruttori panasiatica” che sono “collegati alle reti dandelion”.


Le relazioni tra watershed e aziende sono generalmente da guerra fredda.


“Compriamo ancora da loro, saltuariamente… Cose che ci servono e che ancora non siamo riusciti a riprodurre con l’ingegneria a ritroso, oppure pratichiamo qualche scambio nella speranza di indurli a unirsi a noi. Quando succede, lasciamo che visitino le watershed, purché promettano di comportarsi bene.”


Nel loro rapporto con le aziende, il compito principale delle watershed è la gestione del declino: cercano di rilevarne le funzioni indispensabili rimanenti e mantenere i contatti così da indurle a cambiare la propria cultura, prevenendo ogni azione disperata di retroguardia che farebbe molte vittime.


Non scompariranno presto; dobbiamo continuare a parlare con loro o non cambieranno mai abbastanza da unirsi a noi…


“Abbiamo ancora bisogno di loro. Quando avevano il potere per poco non distruggevano il pianeta; ma fabbricano ancora delle parti importanti per la nostra infrastruttura. Loro pensano di aver bisogno di noi perché senza quelle esportazioni perderebbero la ragione d’esistere. In realtà, questo legame esile è la loro ultima possibilità. Ogni contatto serve a ricordare loro che c’è un’altra strada …

title: Apply Heat, Melt ICE: Flashpoints in the Fight : A Guide to Resisting ICE around the Country this October
content:
All around the United States, people are organizing to resist the federal mercenaries who carry out Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Here, we announce three upcoming mobilizations and share reports from two recent confrontations.


In

Arizona

, people have been blocking the construction of the border wall since July 27; they are calling for people from around the country to come join them. In the

Twin Cities

, people are calling for a countrywide day of action on October 3 to express solidarity with the Minnesota 15, who have been federally charged for allegedly conspiring to resist Operation Metro Surge. In

Vermont

, people have organized a week of action for October 4-9 and are inviting people to come participate or carry out solidarity actions elsewhere. Clashes with federal mercenaries have recently broken out in

Austin, Texas

 and

Frederick, Maryland

.


Awareness of the harm that ICE is inflicting on communities peaked in January, during the

massive popular resistance

 against the federal occupation of the Twin Cities. Yet deportations have only

increased

 since then, with most of the abductions taking place behind closed doors as ICE agents work with police and jails to capture immigrants. The recent wave of resistance to ICE offers a crucial chance to take the offensive ahead of what is bound to be a tumultuous fall.


As many liberals shift to focusing on the midterm elections this November, naïvely hoping that elections alone will provide change, it is especially important to continue to focus on what we can accomplish directly by means of collective power. However the elections turn out, only effective grassroots action can create a situation in which neither party will be able to continue the violence of ICE.


Remember, the abduction and deportation of immigrants

did not begin under Donald Trump

; as recently as last year,

mainstream Democrats

 were proposing to

adopt

 Trump’s xenophobic policies wholesale. Even if the far right loses control of the government, whoever inherits state power will maintain every repressive policy that we do not force them to discontinue. The victory that the movement against ICE achieved in the Twin Cities, forcing Trump to end Operation Metro Surge and fire ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials, shows what we can accomplish when we don’t wait on politicians.


It is time to shift from

reactive

 to

proactive

—from organizing rapid response networks to seizing the initiative. Pick the struggle that is nearest to you geographically or politically and participate in it, whether by traveling to join it or by organizing a local action in solidarity.


Wherever you are, you are probably close to ICE infrastructure, ICE profiteers, or a current hotspot in this struggle. Make plans to travel to a flashpoint near you or organize something at a relevant local target. You can help to boost all of the other events by mentioning all of them in your messaging.


Apply heat, melt ICE!


Minnesota


Out of the tens of thousands who participated in

resisting

 Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota between December and February 2026,

fifteen people

 have been federally charged for allegedly conspiring to resist the violence that ICE agents inflicted on their communities.


The Minnesota 15 Anti-Repression Committee is calling for

a nationwide day of solidarity actions on Saturday, October 3

 to express support for the defendants and all those targeted by ICE. Plan an action at your local ICE office or federal building!


In Minneapolis, on October 3, a labor-led march will traverse downtown to show solidarity with the defendants and to call out the federal government and their corporate enablers. Meet at Peavey Plaza, 1101 Nicollet Mall.


Vermont


From October 4-9, in Chittenden County, Vermont, people will host a week of mass action to end ICE surveillance, targeting, and separation. Everyone is invited!


Vermont is a national nerve center for ICE surveillance. Through the Law Enforcement Support Center and the National Criminal Analysis Targeting Center, both of which are located in Williston, Vermont, ICE collects tips on our immigrant neighbors, spies on civilian social media accounts, and builds lists of targets for kidnapping and deportation. Alongside a dozen other offices scattered around Chittenden County, these sites provide the bureaucratic backbone and surveillance infrastructure for ICE activity countrywide.
